extracted.intended_audience: high-school students preparing for mathematical olympiads, coaches, contest organizers, and teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions and procedural/format standards for national (China) and international (IMO) mathematical olympiad contests: test formats, scoring, selection pipeline, jury/marking procedures, topics, and selection consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMO contest format (paper structure and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IMO test paper consists of 6 questions in all. The actual competition lasts for 2 days for a total of 9 hours where participants are required to complete 3 questions each day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each contest day contains 3 problems to be solved in 4.5 hours. This is the canonical timing/structure organizers and contestants should use for preparation and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMO individual scoring and team total
rubrics_metrics.description: Each question is 7 marks which total up to 42 marks (per contestant). The full score for a team is 252 marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 7-point grading scale per problem when converting solutions to numeric scores; team totals are sum of six contestants' scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medal allocation and special awards at IMO
rubrics_metrics.description: About half of the participants will be awarded a medal, where 1/12 will be awarded a gold medal. The numbers of gold, silver and bronze medals awarded are in the ratio of 1:2:3 approximately. In the case when a participant provides a better solution than the official answer, a special award is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medal cutoffs are decided by the jury (see cut-off criterion entry); special awards may be given for superior/novel solutions beyond official solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMO delegation composition and host responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: All participating countries are required to send a delegation consisting of a leader, a deputy leader and 6 contestants. Each participating country will take turn to host the IMO; the host country bears the cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Host country organizes logistics and the international jury; host does not supply final competition problems (problems are contributed by participating countries and shortlisted by the host for submission to the international jury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem submission, shortlisting and selection process for IMO
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems are contributed by participating countries and are later selected carefully by the host country for submission to the international jury. Eventually, only 6 problems will be accepted for use in the competition. The host country does not provide any question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Host shortlists contributed problems (often many tens of proposals) and submits them to the jury; the jury selects the final 6. Problems may need simplification/ modification/translation prior to submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation responsibilities for IMO problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The short-listed problems are subsequently translated, if necessary, in English, French, German, Russian and other working languages. After that, the team leaders will translate the problems into their own languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate translation is essential; the jury and coordinators check translations and standardize replies to written queries during the contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking procedure and coordinators' role at IMO
rubrics_metrics.description: The answer scripts of each participating team will be marked by the team leader and the deputy leader. The team leader will later present the scripts of their contestants to the coordinators for assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinators (nominated by the host) assess marking, ensure accuracy and fairness, and arbitrate differences between team leaders' marks and the standardized marking scheme; discrepancies can be settled by the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury responsibilities and determination of medal cutoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury is formed by the various team leaders and an appointed chairman by the host country. The jury is responsible for deciding the final 6 problems for the competition. Their duties also include finalizing the marking standard, ensuring the accuracy of the translation of the problems, standardizing replies to written queries raised by participants during the competition, synchronizing differences in marking between the leaders and the coordinators and also deciding on the cut-off points for the medals depending on the difficulties of problems each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must set unified marking standards and final medal cutoffs that reflect problem difficulty; they also resolve marking disputes and approve official clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: China Mathematical Competition (CMC) format and scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: The test paper consists of 6 choices, 6 blanks and 3 questions to be solved with complete process. The full score is 150 marks. Besides, 3 questions are used in the Extra Test, with 50 marks each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMC combines objective (choices/blanks) and full-solution problems; Extra Test problems are each high-value (50 marks) and used for further ranking/selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: China Mathematical Olympiad (CMO / Winter Camp) format and scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: CMO (Winter Camp) lasts for five days. Both the type and the difficulty of the problems match those of IMO. Similarly, they solve three problems every day in four and half hours. However, the score for each problem is 21 marks which add up to 126 marks in total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMO mirrors IMO in timing and problem difficulty but uses 21-point-per-problem scoring; team championships (Chern Shiing-Shen Cup) may be awarded based on aggregate scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese national team selection pipeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Through the China Mathematical Competition, about 120 students are selected to join the China Mathematical Olympiad (CMO) in January. From CMO, about 20 to 30 students are selected to form a national training team. The training lasts for two weeks in March every year. After six to eight tests, plus two qualifying examinations, six students are finally selected to form the national team to take part in IMO in July that year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is staged: mass national contest → CMO (winter camp) → training + testing → final qualifiers. Multiple tests and qualifying rounds are used to narrow candidates to final six.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional/gender-targeted olympiads and selection rules
rubrics_metrics.description: China Western Mathematical Olympiad (from 2001) and China Girls’ Mathematical Olympiad (from 2002) are conducted; the top two winners of these contests will be admitted directly to the national training team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These events serve as targeted recruitment to diversify geographic and gender representation on the national training team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives and scale of China Mathematical Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives: to increase interest of students in learning mathematics, to promote development of co-curricular activities in mathematics, to help improve teaching of mathematics in high schools, to discover and cultivate talents and prepare for IMO. Currently there are about 200,000 participants taking part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The competition is both talent-identification and broad educational outreach; large participation numbers imply multi-stage filtering for selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prizes and direct-admission consequences in national contests
rubrics_metrics.description: The participants with high total marks in the China Mathematical Competition plus the Extra Test are awarded the first prize (about 1,000 participants around China), and they will be admitted into the university directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-ranking contestants receive concrete academic advantages (direct university admission) in addition to awards; prize allocation influences contestants' and schools' incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics typically covered in olympiad problem setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical topics in the IMO include number theory, inequalities, graph theory, polynomials, functional equations, complex numbers, combinatorics, geometry and game theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem setters and trainers should ensure coverage and depth across these classical olympiad areas when preparing problems and training students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality criteria for problem setting and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Good problem preparation involves simplification and modification of candidate problems, recommending top items to the jury (example: China simplified/modified over 100 problems and recommended 28 problems, from which the jury selected), and ensuring high quality in problem statements and translations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem quality is judged by originality, clarity, appropriate difficulty level relative to contest, and translatability; extensive pre-selection and editing are standard practice.
